The Ericeira GazetteNo. 12 · November 2026

Fewer properties, prices holding steady at €5,000/m²

Ericeira has fewer properties for sale than when this record began. In November 2026, 425 properties were advertised, about 24% fewer than in December 2025.

Asking prices have been steadier. The median advertised price is €5,000 per square metre of living space, unchanged from October 2026 and up 7.9% since December 2025. The median is the midpoint: half of the comparable listings ask more per square metre and half ask less.

The homes available also keep changing. In the latest monthly comparison, 65 new listings appeared while 75 disappeared. A property leaving the market does not necessarily mean it sold; it may have been withdrawn, expired or returned under a different advert.

Some individual sellers changed their expectations. Among properties advertised in both October 2026 and November 2026, 27 reduced their asking price, compared with 10 increases.

For buyers, the picture is mixed. There are fewer properties to choose from and asking prices remain above the start of this record. But the reductions show that not every seller is holding firm, so homes previously dismissed as too expensive may be worth checking again.

Prices shown are advertised asking prices, not final sale prices.

Key takeaway
  • Homes built since 2020 are the most expensive, asking €5,916/m², 14% above their local zone.
  • Homes built between 2000 and 2009 are the cheapest at €4,118/m², 17% below their zone.
  • Older homes are not necessarily cheaper. Properties built between 1980 and 1999 also command a premium of 7%.
  • Homes built between 2010 and 2019 are considerably larger (typically 202 m²), partly explaining their lower price per m².

Bottom line: Recent construction commands a clear premium, but the relationship between age and price is not linear.

256 of 425 listings state the year built (60%), and 218 of them also state Área Útil, so the €/m² figures rest on 218. Years from 2024 are new builds, some still under construction (the latest stated year is 2027).
Groups with fewer than 20 listings (Before 1980, 2010 to 2019) are less reliable.

Four different kinds of information, kept apart below:
  1. Terrace and balcony: stated by the listing as a type (283 of 425), never in m².
  2. Plot size: stated in m² (201 listings, houses).
  3. Garden and pool: not a data field at all, only words in the ad text.
  4. Living space vs. Extra Bruta area: living area, Extra Bruta area and plot.

1. Terrace and balcony · stated in the listing

A data field: the listing says whether the home has a terrace, a balcony or both, but never how big. ‘Not stated’ means the field is empty, not that there is none.
Key takeaway
  • A terrace on its own goes with a higher price: €5,462/m², 9% above comparable homes.
  • A balcony does not raise the price: €4,866/m², 4% below comparable homes.

2. Plot size (m²)

Plot size is stated for 201 listings, mostly houses. Land is a small part of the price: built area and location do most of the work.
Key takeaway
  • Only plots of 600 to 1,200 m² stand out: -15% against comparable homes (28 listings).
  • Doubling the plot size adds only about 6% to the total asking price.
iAsking price against plot size for the 201 listings that state one. Along the trend, doubling the plot raises the asking price by about 6%.
iEach home's price per m² compared with the typical price per m² of its own zone. 0% means the same as its zone, +10% means it asks 10% more per m² than the typical home of its zone. Red = asks more than its zone, green = asks less. Size is not taken out: smaller homes ask more per m², so they often sit above 0%.

3. Garden and pool · only mentioned in the ad

Listings have no data field for these. We searched each ad’s text for the words ‘jardim’ (garden) and ‘piscina’ (pool): ‘Ad mentions it’ means the word appears, ‘Ad does not mention it’ means it does not. A mention is not proof (‘near the beach’, ‘no pool’), so read the gaps as hints.
Key takeaway
  • Mentioning a garden goes with a lower price (-8 points); mentioning a pool goes with a lower price (-8 points).
  • Against comparable homes, garden: -7% when mentioned, +1% when not; pool: -6% when mentioned, +2% when not. A mention is not proof, so treat it as a hint.

4. Living space vs. Extra Bruta area

Not all built area is living space. Across 324 listings reporting both areas, a typical home has 44 m² of Extra Bruta area, representing 23% of its total built area. A typical detached house has 196 m² of living space, 60 m² of Extra Bruta area and a 509 m² plot. More on the Living Space tab.
Key takeaway
  • About 23% of a home's total built area is Extra Bruta area, with similar proportions across house types (22% to 25%).
  • Homes with more Extra Bruta area tend to ask slightly more per m². Those with at least 35% Extra Bruta area command a 9% premium compared with similar homes in the same zone.
iExtra Bruta area = Área Bruta minus Área Útil. It includes built space not counted as living area, such as garages, storage and other ancillary areas. Each bar is a typical house of that type: its living area (Útil) plus its Extra Bruta area, which together make the total built area (Área Bruta). Middle values of each part, so the stack is approximate.
iThe land the house stands on, for listings that state a plot. Not part of the built area, so it has its own chart and its own scale.
iHomes grouped by the share of Extra Bruta area in their total built area. Price per m² is the asking price divided by the living area (Útil).
iEach home's price per m² compared with the typical price per m² of its own zone. 0% means the same as its zone, +10% means it asks 10% more per m² than the typical home of its zone. Red = asks more than its zone, green = asks less. Size is not taken out: smaller homes ask more per m², so they often sit above 0%.
* Median: the middle value, so half the homes are above it and half below.
% Extra price per m²: % above (+) or below (−) comparable homes, meaning the median of the same area of Ericeira (Norte, Sul, Centro, Nascente). 0% = same as comparable homes.
Key takeaway
  • Homes between 1 km and 1.5 km from the sea command the highest prices, typically €5,279/m².
  • Location matters more than distance alone. Some neighbourhoods farther from the coast are more expensive than those closer to it.
  • Homes farther inland also tend to be larger, partly explaining their lower price per m².

Bottom line: The neighbourhood and the size of the home also influence prices.

425 of 425 listings have a location, and 324 of them also state Área Útil, so the €/m² figures rest on 324. Distance is a straight line to the coast and is approximate, so read it in steps of 0.5 km.

Transaction price per m², rolling 12 months

Median €/m² of sales completed in the previous 12 months, updated quarterly.

INE official data, Q4 2019 to Q2 2026
  • INE measures completed property transactions, not asking prices.
  • Each quarterly figure is a rolling 12-month median of transaction-level €/m², based on Área Bruta Privativa.
  • Asking and completed-sale figures are not directly comparable: they cover different properties, area definitions and periods.

Source: INE, Instituto Nacional de Estatística. Estatísticas de preços da habitação ao nível local, indicator 0012234: median sales value in the last 12 months (€/m²), methodology 2022. Figures as published by INE.

INE methodology and data sources
  • Completed sales, not asking prices. INE builds these figures from tax records of completed property purchases (the property transfer tax, linked to the property register).
  • Medians of transaction-level prices. INE divides the price of every sale of a home of 20 m² or more by its area and reports the middle value.
  • Área Bruta Privativa. The area is the private floor area measured to the outer wall perimeter and wall axes, including enclosed private balconies, basements and attics used like the home.
  • Each point covers the preceding 12 months. Neighbouring points share nine months of sales, so a point is not a quarterly or monthly price.
  • Updated quarterly, with a lag. INE publishes about three and a half months after a quarter ends and sometimes revises earlier figures.
  • Ericeira is INE’s area, not our four zones. The asking-price zones used elsewhere on this site (Centro da Vila, Ericeira Norte, Sul and Nascente) may not match INE’s boundary exactly.
  • Areas. Mafra municipality includes Ericeira. Lisbon and Cascais are municipalities. INE publishes a figure only for areas with at least 33 sales.
  • Not comparable with asking prices. Completed sales and listings cover different homes, areas, measurement conventions and periods, so the gap between them cannot be read as a negotiated discount.

About Erireal

I live in Ericeira and started digging into the property market while planning my own house project.

I found that homes were hard to compare. Ads do not always describe space in the same way, useful information can be missing, and asking prices do not tell the whole story.

I built Erireal to make the market easier to understand.

The numbers show how asking prices and the number of properties for sale are changing. You can compare listings, find them on a map and see which homes ask less per m² than similar homes.

I’m Seb, a portfolio manager and data analyst living in Ericeira. Erireal is an independent personal project, made for educational purposes only. It has no commercial purpose: I’m just a data analyst sharing what the numbers show. I’m not an estate agent, and nothing here is advice.

Get in touch →

Why homes are hard to compare

Sale prices are rarely published in Portugal, and property ads do not always measure space in the same way. Even the price per m² can be misleading because the advertised area may include garages, terraces, storage and other space that you cannot live in.

When an ad provides it, Erireal uses Área Útil: the space you can actually live in. This makes it easier to compare one home with another and understand the asking price per m² of living space.

Who is this for?

Erireal is for anyone who wants to understand the Ericeira property market, whether they are buying, selling, working as an agent or simply curious.

The site compares advertised homes with one another. It does not decide what a home is worth.

Methodology

All prices on this site are asking prices taken from public listings. They are not recorded transaction prices.
Data source
Public listings for houses and apartments for sale in the area, read from the search results and from each listing page.
Update frequency
Monthly. Each month uses the first complete scrape of that month; tracking started in December 2025.
Geographic scope
The scrape covers the whole Mafra municipality. Every tab except Zones is restricted to the Ericeira parish (freguesia), taken from the location in each listing’s title. The Zones tab shows all of Mafra, grouped by the zone assigned to each listing.
Inclusion
Every listing returned by the search for properties for sale in the area, whatever the asking price or size.
Deduplication
One row per listing ID per month. The same home advertised by two agencies under two IDs is counted twice; relisting detection is not applied yet.
How Área Útil is extracted
From the characteristics block of each listing page, where agencies state “m² úteis” (Área Útil) and “m² área bruta” (Área Bruta). Values are read as published, including thousands separators.
€/m² Área Útil
For each listing, asking price divided by Área Útil. The headline figure is the median across every listing that reports Área Útil. €/m² Área Bruta is computed the same way, across every listing that reports Área Bruta.
Área Útil vs Área Bruta
Área Útil is the actual living space. Área Bruta is the advertised gross area and can include walls, garages, terraces, storage and other non-living areas, so €/m² on Área Bruta understates what living space costs and varies with how much extra area a listing includes.
Missing areas and sample coverage
Each €/m² median uses every listing that reports that area. Listings missing an area are left out of that median only; they stay in the counts and in the median asking price. This month 424 of 425 listings (100%) report Área Bruta and 324 (76%) report Área Útil, so the two KPIs are based on different samples.
Methodology change, October 2026
Before this correction both medians were computed only on listings reporting both areas. Listings that give only Área Bruta tend to ask more per m², so that rule understated the Área Bruta median (by 2% to 8% in individual months) and exaggerated its rise. Each median now uses all listings with that area, and every month since December 2025 has been recalculated the same way. The Área Útil series is unchanged, because every listing reporting Área Útil also reports Área Bruta.
Median changes
Monthly medians can repeat or jump when the middle of the distribution lands on the same listing. Treat changes over several months as more meaningful than a single month.
New listing
A listing ID present this month and absent from last month’s scrape.
Removed listing
A listing ID present last month and absent this month. It may have been sold, withdrawn, expired or relisted under a new ID. It is not treated as a sale.
Price change
A listing present in both months whose asking price changed by more than 0.5%.
First seen / months tracked
Scraping is monthly, so time on the market is counted in months in which the listing appeared. Listings already online in Dec '25 may have been listed earlier.
Email updates
Signing up for the monthly update collects only your email address, used solely to send that update. It is stored by Buttondown, the service Erireal uses to send it, not by any other party. Every email includes an unsubscribe link.
Visit counts
Page views are counted with GoatCounter, a privacy-friendly counter that sets no cookies and does not track you across sites or store personal data.
